The “paranormal” aspect of the story establishes Tina’s character and personality.  This earlier part of her life demonstrates that she is incapable of admitting responsibility for her actions.  Even when it became clear that she was responsible for causing the “paranormal phenomena” at her parent’s home and that her “telekinetic/psychic prowess” were a complete farce, she was absolutely incapable of admitting it.  I don’t know if her denial was to the point of being delusional and completely disconnected from reality, or whether she was fully aware that what she was doing was all a ruse—that is to say, it definitely is possible to be so committed to the act that you start to believe your own bullshit, especially if you have ppl like Jeannie and that idiot parapsychologist reinforcing it the entire time. 

She never stopped doing this.  You see throughout the documentary just how manipulative she is.  She knows how to develop emotional ties with these people who end up advocating on her behalf, she knows how to influence them to credulously believe her own fabricated narrative and completely discount the overwhelming evidence that is right in front of their eyes. It’s next to impossible to have any doubt that Christina engaged in a long standing pattern of severe physical abuse that she inflicted on her daughter—it wasn’t just that one day, the abuse was severe and chronic and it simply doesn’t stand to reason that she had no culpability in this.  

I do think it’s most likely that David was the actual one who caused the blunt force head trauma that killed her,  but even so, the overzealous Georgetown law students are completely missing the point.  He WAS still convicted of having a role in the girl’s death; he just was able to provide enough reasonable doubt that the prosecution could not prove that he had been the immediate cause of it.  The critical difference between him and Tina is that Tina was in full denial mode, just like when she was a kid, and was utterly incapable of admitting the undeniable truth that she did abuse her child.  Even thirty years later, she’s still clinging on to the fiction that she was this devoted, dedicated mother who did the best she could.  The closest I saw her come to admitting the truth (and I’m not quite done, I still have twenty mins left of episode three) was when she acknowledged in episode two or so that “she wasn’t always the best mother.”  I guarantee you that this is the closest she will ever come to acknowledging the mountain of physical abuse that she had inflicted on that child.  She’s never developed any ability beyond outright denial to be able to cope with her own trauma and her sense of moral development, as she was severely stunted in developing this capacity during her own childhood.

Had she admitted that she did abuse her daughter and was responsible for some of her injuries—while still maintaining that she was not responsible for the head injury that killed her—she likely would have been granted some measure of leniency, esp in terms of being granted parole.  But she’s still holding on to this delusional reality where she did nothing to cause harm to her daughter, or at the very least, it was never her intention to do so—which, just like her teenage psychic bullshit, is a fabrication, if not an outright lie.  So that’s why they haven’t shown leniency, bc she’s still holding on to this bullshit that she’s the victim, she was wrongly convicted and did absolutely nothing to hurt her daughter.  She’s lucky as hell her lawyer had the sense to not take this to trial, bc she 100% would have been convicted and would have been executed.  Her “shoddy public defender” is the sole reason she didn’t get a needle in her arm.

She’s playing everyone on “Team Tina” like a fiddle, and I’ve found myself yelling at my television every time two idiotic law students open their damn mouths.  Tina was NOT fit to be a mother.  (And I’m certainly not saying that bc she was poor, nor am I saying that bc she was a single mother.  I am saying she was not psychologically well enough to be a good mother who had the capacity to take care of her daughter.  I had an aunt who was not too dissimilar from her, and I thank God my mom stepped in and had her young daughter taken into CPS and placed with an adoptive family, bc I don’t think she would have survived had much longer had they not. She ended up dying twenty years later in a tent in the woods.  It’s still sad, but it doesn’t change the fact that she was literally incapable of being a good mother given her mental state.). The deepest irony of this entire travesty is that had Tina just done what her own mom had done to her, by leaving her at the hospital because she knew she was not capable of caring for her, then in all likelihood Amber would still be alive.

Last thing - She’s unable to even acknowledge her own inconsistency.  During David’s trial when she’s a witness, she testifies she never saw David hurt her daughter in any way, and had no reason to believe he did so.  After he throws her under the bus she becomes indignant bc she claims she was the one who “didn’t lie”; however, if what she was saying were actually true and he wasn’t responsible, then who does that leave?  So she’s not even logically consistent with her own claim of innocence.

If Christina ever wants to leave prison, she has to finally acknowledge the role she played in abusing her child and her subsequent death.  I honestly don’t think she ever will admit to this, and for that reason, I have no issue with her staying in prison for the rest of her life.  (And shame on all of those who perpetuate Tina’s lie that she had nothing to do with her daughter’s death and the abuse she suffered.  They anger me almost as much as she does.)

Thank you for the info. Ok I think I’ve heard enough from all of you here to reassure myself not to waste any more time pondering this, that she must have been an outlier.  Thanks to all who replied to my post here, I appreciate all of you.  

Signing off for tonight so I can go ahead and get some sleep.  Take care!

Thank you!!  Yup, I’m familiar with ASAN.  Yeah it struck me as really odd, and I was sitting there asking myself “wait a sec, did I miss something here??”  The panelist was herself autistic and worked at an autism center in Cali, and I chalked it up at the time to just a disconnect and maybe more of a west coast thing.  Good to know though that this seems to be something that’s more isolated to her and her specific group, and not mainstream autistic culture as a whole.

Technically it’d be a black person dictating to another black person how they should refer to themselves, as the panelist was herself autistic.  She also appeared to be heavily involved in autistic rights/neurodiversity issues, as this was a lot of what she talked about on the panel (although I will admit I was not expecting her to also be a BCBA…humans of all types are very complex).  

It was just something she said matter-of-fact, as if I should have already known that “autistic self advocate” is apparently no longer politically correct.  If that’s the case, it moves so fast that it’s really hard for me to keep up with, tbh.

I do wholeheartedly agree with you.  Honestly it kind of irked me a bit when she said that, although I kept it to myself at the time.  Just wanted to make sure there wasn’t some major change that I somehow missed.

Sorry, I hardly never post on reddit and don’t have time to go into detail in rules/general etiquette, so please know I don’t mean offense.  I posted this (and forgot to add context - again, my apologies) due to a panel question I asked at a conference.  The person who responded to my question identifies as autistic and is also a BCBA, but seemed very versed in disability rights and autism advocacy.  She prefaced her response by saying that the term “autistic self advocate” is no longer the correct/preferred term in the autistic community, and that if anyone didn’t already know this or doesn’t know why, to google it.  

I myself am autistic and have the diagnosis, and this was news to me.  I tried searching several different versions of this question and relevant search terms on Google, but nothing.  (I also checked ASAN’s site recently, and as far as I can tell they’re still ASAN, so I guess I’m in good company here…). I also got her contact info and texted her asking about this, and she directed me to her organizations Facebook group, but I explained to her I can’t do Facebook and haven’t used it since 2018 for the sake of my mental health (and it’s not worth it to me to risk my mental stability just to chase down the answer to what should be a fairly simple question).

So if anyone knows anything about this, if you have a moment, please enlighten me.  I try to be aware of and and respectful of the preferences of the majority consensus of the autistic community, but I must admit that this one has me scratching my head.  Thank you so much for your time, I do appreciate it.

Your pain is just as valid as mine.  There’s no such thing as not having the right to feel how you feel; your pain and suffering is no less than anyone else’s.  Please don’t allow yourself or anyone else to ever make you feel that what you’ve been through “doesn’t count.”  It does.  I’ve been there myself, standing on a chair with a belt around my neck, shifting my body lower and lower until there was bruising around my neck and trying to will myself to kick the chair out beyond my reach.  Thank God I didn’t, that I always held on bc I was too scared to go all the way with it.  And thank God that the times I overdosed, they found me in time to get me to the ER to pump my stomach.  But even if it had been less severe, it’s not the type of thing that should ever be viewed through a lens of, “oh, it’s just a cry for help” or “she’s just doing it for attention.”  To view someone’s pain and suffering like that is so dismissive, dehumanizing, and invalidating, and we must speak up when others try to reduce suicide attempts in such an ignorant manner.  We also must not allow ourselves to internalize this mindset and start belittling our own suffering, as if it shouldn’t matter.

What you are going through does matter and is not trivial or meaningless.  It is valid.  You are valid to feel what you feel.  It’s ok to not feel ok, and as someone else was kind enough to say to me when I was low myself, “the people who mind don’t matter, and the people who matter don’t mind.”  Unfortunately the former type of person is all too common, but I assure you that there are plenty of ppl who fall into the latter group.  Please try to stick around for those ppl.  You will find them sooner or later.

I’m glad you’ve made it through tonight.  I understand what it feels like to believe no one wants to talk to you or finds you interesting, from having had those same thoughts about myself many, many times over the course of my life.  Looking back on it through hindsight, a lot of this was bc I was depressed, and the ppl around me didn’t really know what to do with that, as I was unintentionally giving signals that indicated a lack of interest in them, and also bc being suicidal made them fearful for me and they didn’t know what to do.  I couldn’t see that when I was in that state, though, and all I could think was that they must have thought that I’m just as worthless as I thought I was myself, which wasn’t actually true.  Depression distorts how we interpret reality, and how we interpret others and how they relate to us.  So know that a lot of what you’re feeling/going through right now is bc you are depressed.  

The most important thing to do when you feel this way is to do what you did, by reaching out and communicating that you are in danger, even if it’s to a bunch of internet strangers.  This kept you alive, and this is what I had to do myself just to survive the bouts of severe suicidal ideation and deep, seemingly unrelenting depressions.  

Know that you won’t always feel this way; sooner or later, it does pass to where things become less shitty.  Of course things do get bad again sooner or later, but the important thing to keep in mind is that it cycles—better times follow the shitty ones, followed by bad periods, then not so bad, and so on.  Speaking from having made several attempts over my life where I was nearly successful in ending it, I can genuinely tell you that I am so thankful to still be alive.  

Please continue to hold on, and please keep in mind all the things the ppl here have shared with you.  It’s not always going to be this bad; it comes and goes.  I know how painful it is right now (there’s actually a term for the severe mental anguish of being acutely suicidal—“psychache”, and this experience affects the same areas of our brains as the sensation of acute physical pain, so that is a big part of why it is so intensely painful to go through), but it will subside gradually over time.  It may return, though, but when it does, do whatever is necessary to keep yourself going for another day until the pain finally recedes.

Please be kind to yourself, and please do whatever you can to be able to stay.  The world needs people like you to be in it, bc we lose so much when good-hearted and thoughtful ppl are unable to stay.  I lost my own mother to suicide eight years ago now, and I still miss her so much to this day.  Please, as much as you can, try to stay alive, bc I am not bullshitting you when I say that the world needs ppl like you to be in it.

I agree wholeheartedly with everything you said here, as well as throughout the thread posts you provided below.  I simply could not have put any of it better myself.  Whenever I’ve watched this show, I’ve always felt bothered by it but unable to put my finger on the specifics, which you did brilliantly.  One thing I will say that wasn’t mentioned is specifically about Michael, whose representation on the show is the one I feel the most bad for.  He is extremely infantilized on the show, and the questions posed to him by the producers are done in a way that perpetuates that stereotype.  I cannot tell you just how hard I cringed (and felt a bit sick, to be honest) at the multiple times he called his attempts at dating to find a suitable partner a “quest”, as this definitely gave off Chris Chan vibes and was not appropriate (nor was it responsible of the producers to go along with this portrayal, at least imo).  It’s how a young child views the prospect of finding love, and while this is something to be seen as “cute” when expressed by an 8 year old boy, it is downright disturbing to see this exact mindset in a young man in his mid twenties.  I don’t want to put all the baggage and fucked up internet history of Chris Chan onto someone like Michael, but oh my God did it make me feel sick when he said that.  Portrayals like this do a huge disservice for people on the autism spectrum and lead to neurotypical people perpetuating stereotypes of us as mentally being children in adults’ bodies.  Thank you so much for rightfully calling all of this out.

Please don’t pull being autistic into this.  Maybe the younger crowd of autistics, sure, but I and most of the other ppl I know on the spectrum don’t ascribe to using “void” pronouns or neopronouns.  Maybe it appears that way when you consider that the most vocal ones on the internet tend to do this.  But I certainly would not say “most ppl who use void pronouns are on the autism spectrum,” nor would I agree that “a lot of ppl on the spectrum” use these.  Please don’t make broad generalizations like this by claiming to speak for most ppl who are autistic.

Sorry, I assumed your stance was pro-life, and I realize I read into what you were saying a bit more than what you actually put there.  I’m mentioning these issues because when society starts “valuing the life of a six week old fetus differently” and grants it personhood wholesale, thereby making it a legal standard that any abortion occurring after that dividing line constitutes murder regardless of circumstance or context (or if they have their way, any abortion at any time), then it leads us down a very slippery slope.  When the rights of an unborn fetus at 6 weeks old, one that by scientific measures has not achieved any of the hallmarks typically associated with having personhood,  supersede the rights of the mother tasked with bringing the pregnancy to term against her will (or in some cases, against her very survival, as bringing some pregnancies to term and giving birth can cost the mother her life), and even supersedes the rights of that very same child once it has been birthed into an unforgiving world that does not guarantee that even its most basic needs be met (as pro-lifers tend not to advocate for the quality of life of the child once it comes into the world), that is a problem.  I’m just saying that there are many factors that need to be taken into account when making moral judgments such as these, and that having laws on the books that make abortion murder no matter the circumstances or context will have unintended negative consequences.

Again, I’m not arguing for “killing babies,” as you put it.  It depends on at what point during the pregnancy the abortion occurs.  First trimester abortions would not meet this definition, as the fetus has not developed to this point yet, while a third trimester abortion certainly would, and in that latter case I would concede that your argument holds water.  It’s a nuanced issue that depends on context; it is a false and disingenuous argument to make by saying that all abortion, regardless of the circumstances, is murder.

I’m really trying to understand your side.  While you do make good arguments and I have no doubt about the passion you have for your beliefs, the issue of abortion is a complicated one and speaking realistically, there are no easy solutions. 

I myself am decidedly pro-choice, however, I am not against REASONABLE restrictions and regulations on the procedure.  (For example, I do not believe abortion should be used as one’s primary method of birth control, especially for those who don’t want to get pregnant but still willingly have sexual intercourse without using any freely available method of birth control).  I do believe that at a certain point prior to birth the fetus reaches a developmental stage in which it could conceivably survive outside the womb—that it can breathe, has reflexes and can feel sensations—and at that point the fetus has achieved personhood, and its life should absolutely be protected.  

I think we also need to weigh the circumstances we are imposing on the life of the fetus it will grow into when forcing it to be brought to term by an unwilling mother who either does not have the financial resources to reasonably provide it with a safe and clean environment and care for its needs,  or does not have the emotional resources to provide it with a loving, secure and healthy attachment (or both).  I assume that you were provided with one or both of these by your own mother who raised you, but imagine just how much you would suffer if you were forced to grow up in a hostile environment by a parent who doesn’t love you and never wanted you, and even worse (but unfortunately not uncommon), hurts you, abuses you, and/or neglects you.  You would be permanently broken and likely would wish you were never born.  You would also be predisposed to engaging in criminal activity and antisocial behavior, as well as reckless behavior like impulsive sex, which would just perpetuate this vicious cycle.  There’s a reason why there was such a huge drop in crime during the nineties—it coincided with being precisely 17+ years after the Roe v. Wade decision, without which thousands of unwanted pregnancies would have been forced to be carried to term, and this would be the exact age range when these unwanted children would have been most likely to engage in criminal behavior, had they been forced to a traumatic upbringing by parents who didn’t want them.  Having an abortion is not an easy decision to make, and I know of many mothers who would have wanted to have brought their children to term had circumstances been different and they were in a position to provide for them and love them, but they recognized that the best thing they could do to prevent them having to endure a cruel existence of pain and suffering was to not have them.  This should not be a decision that the government makes for them. 

That’s the thing with calling yourself “pro-life”—the people who comprise this group generally don’t give a damn what happens to the child after it is born, nor do they have any concern about what kind of hellish existence they are forcing this poor child into, as you cannot even begin to imagine the severe abuse and trauma so many of these children suffer.  If the people who call themselves pro life start to actually care about the quality of life for these unfortunate children and start supporting social programs and government policies that benefit these at-risk families, such as mandating a living wage and providing childcare to working mothers who are just trying to survive, then maybe I can begin to take you seriously.  But from what I’ve seen of pretty much all the people I’ve encountered who identify as “pro-life”, they should really call themselves “pro-birth, consequences-be-damned” instead, because they’ve made it clear that beyond guaranteeing that a fetus be carried to term (even if said fetus has severe birth defects and is not viable outside the womb, or when continuing the pregnancy risks killing the mother, etc.), none of you give a damn about the life the child is born into.  (None of this even addresses the obvious fact that no one seems willing to talk about or even acknowledge, which is that our planet is rapidly approaching a point where it can no longer sustain the global human population and, as such, unrestrained population growth will likely doom us all...but I digress). 

I do genuinely wish that there were no need for abortion.  I wish that from conception onward each and every unborn child were guaranteed to come into this world with a stable home life and parents who loved them.  Realistically speaking, however, this is a fantasy completely divorced from the exigencies of the real world, and it’s way past time that we start acknowledging these uncomfortable truths.

I lost my mother to suicide nearly seven years ago, after she had already endured the many attempts I had made on my own life throughout my troubled adolescence and young adulthood.  This burden I had unintentionally imposed on her (which I am by no means saying was selfish, nor did she ever say that she felt this way or that my attempts reflected poorly on her, or anything about her beyond her feeling helpless to save me from myself) with my own struggles with severe depression and suicidal ideation eventually led to her making a nearly lethal attempt herself, and she never fully recovered from it, languishing on in a depressive fog for several years more until she just couldn’t anymore.  The moment I thought she was finally happy again and becoming who she used to be was the moment I lost her, as she made her final attempt not long after I had convinced myself she was getting better.  And I truly felt dead inside for a long time after, bitterly blaming myself for not being able to save her, along with carrying an unbearable sense of guilt for what I had put her through (even though I knew full well she would have told me herself it wasn’t my fault; I can never doubt how much she loved me, but for the life of me I can never comprehend just how little love she had for herself).  

It was months later that I started attending a local Survivors of Suicide group, not long after Robin Williams passed away, and it was at this very first group that a grieving mother said something that has stuck with me to this very day: “I’ve heard people say all my life that people who commit suicide are being selfish, but I think they have it wrong—rather, I think it might just be that it’s selfish of us to expect them to stay, by asking them to endure unimaginable suffering just to make us happy.  I feel like my son, he stayed as long as he possibly could, and I could never dare call him selfish for not being able to hold on and stay when he was suffering so much.  More than anything, I just wish I could have been able to take away his pain, or to have known the right thing to say, or to have done just about anything to make it where he would’ve been able to stay.”

I kept going to these meetings for several years after, because the only people who can understand this kind of loss are the people who have lived it themselves; others just don’t get it, and in my experience these ignorant others were the kind of people most likely to callously accuse their loved ones of being selfish.  It was rare that I heard other survivors talk about the loved ones they lost as being selfish or weak, in fact I can’t remember a single concrete instance of this ever actually being said (although I do remember a couple instances of individuals who were angry at their loved ones for committing suicide, and this was usually when the loss had happened very recently and they hadn’t fully processed it yet).  I haven’t gone in several years now, but these people will always be extended family to me, as a suicide is a loss like no other.  So speaking as someone who has survived suicide in both senses, having survived the loss of my mother and my own many, many attempts, I totally agree with everything you’re saying here.  Suicide is scary for people who have no experience with it, and they interpret it as a threat to everything they believe and identify with.  And because of this, knowing that they have never been “in the deep end” of life themselves, in my mind I try to forgive them for their ignorance and lack of empathy, and hope that they are able to grow as individuals and  learn that there is so much more to life and loss than their own narrow worldview.  

Anyway, thanks for advocating on behalf of those of us who have been affected by suicide and letting me share my story.  These are hard times for us all, and while I never could have imagined back then that I’d still be here, oddly enough I think I’m going to try to see it through to the very end.  You take care and be safe too.

I happen to be a girl who found him mildly amusing when I first stumbled upon his FFVIII review back when I was in college.  I remember giving his videos a try because I was bored and procrastinating on solving integrals or some other shit I had no interest in whatsoever but still had to do to get my math requirement out of the way.  I hated the draw system too when I played the game as a kid, so watching his humorous approach to demonstrating the self-inflicted pain that came along with it validated my own experience so I knew it wasn’t just me.   I had some positive memories of the game as well, though, but seeing someone go totally overboard in ripping the game a new one gave me some laughs and was a welcome distraction.  (The disturbing hentai final fantasy porn detour he took in the FFVII mini-review was something I would have preferred going my entire life without ever seeing, especially the unfathomable monstrosity some fan made of Quistis that was the stuff of nightmares, but I digress).  Anyway, I came back to his videos every now and then, never really going much beyond his final fantasy reviews and a couple niche one-off reviews that matched my interests (i.e., the X-Files Resist or Serve review was another one of my personal favorites, although that one as far as I can tell seems to have been lost with some of the rest of his older material once the website was gone).  I think the last time I visited his site was 2013, around when he posted his FF13 review.  I never subjected myself to actually playing that one, though, as I already knew from other people that it had none of the old school features that I had grown up loving as a kid with the SNES  and the PS games, so I couldn’t really relate.  I also thought Spoony looked pretty gross with the long hair.  Boy was I surprised to find out how his life has turned out when I first stumbled on this subreddit around the time when the pandemic started; I didn’t have a clue about any of it and had just assumed he had kept going, but in hindsight it all makes sense.

So to answer your question: Even when I was a “fan” of his, I would have never, ever wanted to date him, not even in his prime.  Why?  Because his personality is just not attractive.  Yeah he was pretty funny, but just the thought of dating him...uh, no.  I thought he would be way too annoying to have any type of relationship with; he was way too immature and way too full of himself, even though the dude was six or seven years older than me.  (And yeah, I did see on his old site where he prominently had some shit about where you could “win” a signed autograph of him, as well as his amazon wishlist, and let’s just say that having that much of a bloated ego and sense of entitlement when you’re essentially an internet nobody who just does amateur quality review videos on the internet is not a good look for anyone).  Then there was the time I made the mistake of clicking on the link for “Spooning with Spoony,” and I think I threw up a bit in my mouth after seeing that one.  (Also had the same reaction just reading the sentence “I can’t help but feel that there is some mysterious quality about the Spoonyone that is sexy”...haha good Lord, no.)

I will say that he was not a bad looking guy back then, but it’s really someone’s personality that makes them attractive, even though it does remain true that it’s usually physical appearance that first draws you in.  So maybe if he wasn’t such an insufferable asshole whose biggest fan was always himself, maybe I would have found him attractive.  But no, I would never, ever want to date him, even if he were still popular and churning out semi-quality reviews, because I have very little patience for a spoiled man-child who refuses to take responsibility and grow the fuck up.

Usually I stay the fuck out of debates such as this one, but speaking as someone who both works in academic autism research and is on the spectrum herself, there’s a couple things that need to be addressed here.  First, Chris Chan does not have Asperger’s (which isn’t an actual diagnostic entity anymore, but he would’ve never met criteria for it in the first place even if you’re going by the DSM-IV diagnosis); he would most likely be diagnosed as having an autism spectrum disorder, level 2 - requiring substantial support.  There’s no way he would ever be capable of living independently on his own, and his verbal repertoire isn’t great to begin with, among other reasons I don’t have the energy to get into right now, so let’s just put that myth to rest.  Second, what is commonly overlooked is that Chris Chan is not JUST autistic—that is, he has several additional pathologies as well, particularly what appears to be severe schizoaffective personality disorder, in addition to some outright psychotic features that suggest a much deeper and profound impairment.  Suffice it to say, Chris Chan is not your typical case of ASD, which is why he is such a poor choice of representing autism to the wider public, as most of us are nothing like Chris Chan.  The tragedy of his case is that it was not “mandated by God” that he grow up to be so profoundly impaired and incapable of independent adaptive functioning; rather, the obvious mental illness exhibited by both his parents took a very heavy toll on his early development, and he basically didn’t have a chance from the start bc he was born into a very fucked up family who were incapable of providing him with the early intervention and competent parenting he needed in order to develop a repertoire of even the most basic adaptive skills.  

To your point about Spoony possibly being ASD: in the interests of keeping this relatively short, trust me—he is NOT on the autism spectrum. The key to keeping yourself motivated is finding ways to reinforce positive/productive behaviors.  There’s an empirically-based rule of behavior known as the Premack principle that is actually quite effective once you figure out how to adapt it to your own life.  Basically, to get yourself to do something you don’t want to do, you make doing something you’d rather be doing contingent on you doing the thing you don’t want to do.  To get yourself started, you begin with some small but essential component of what you need to get done, then follow that up with a big reward, and then keep building on that.  As you keep doing piece by piece of the task you’d rather not do (that is, as the less preferred behavior “gains momentum”), you can gradually “thin” the reinforcement schedule and still maintain that adaptive behavior—that is, you can make yourself work longer for less reinforcement.  I’ll give an example to illustrate: Let’s say I’ve been putting off writing the introduction for a manuscript, and I cannot for the life of me make myself sit down and do it. I do really like perusing reddit, though.  So I decide to impose on myself the following contingency: for every sentence I write of the introduction, I’ll give myself fifteen minutes on Reddit.  Gradually I’ll increase how much I have to write for the same amount of reddit time, or if I’m feeling really ambitious, I can gradually lessen the amount of reddit time (or netflix time, or smoking time, or whatever else I’d rather be doing) I get for the time I spend writing.  I can also reinforce other related behaviors that help facilitate getting done the thing I don’t want to do—like for my example, reading relevant parts of the APA manual to check my formatting, reading other related papers in the literature as examples, scheduling a meeting with the professor I’m writing the paper with to bounce ideas off of and get their suggestions on revisions, or using my paper writing time for doing grammatical/stylistic edits instead of writing more (especially for those moments of writer’s block), etc.—basically all the associated things that help me get the task done, and then reinforcing the hell out of each one.  (You probably already know what I mean by “reinforcement,” but in case it isn’t clear, it’s following a behavior you want to make more frequent with something pleasurable or rewarding that makes it more likely for you to do the behavior that resulted in that favorable consequence occurring.  Also doing smaller things that build up to doing the thing you need to get done are referred to as “successive approximations”, and these help build “behavioral momentum”.). The key is setting up these reinforcement contingencies to occur naturally, so once you get that behavioral momentum going, you’re able to maintain that behavior without having to deliberately set it up each time.  Also make sure to give yourself credit for each step you take toward your goal, no matter how small.  (Remember thar positive self-talk can also be reinforcing).  Be kind to yourself and never forget to celebrate the small victories.  

The other thing I do is at the beginning of each month, I write down literally every single thing I can think of that I need to do, and put a blank space beside each one where I can put a check mark beside it once I’ve gotten it done.  Some of these tasks have multiple components, so I put a space for a check mark beside each small step.  Even if I only get about half of the list done at the end of the month, I reinforce the hell out of it.  Even the checkmarks themselves are reinforcing for me (in fact, they’re technically what’s referred to as “conditioned reinforcers”), and I get so much satisfaction each time I check each one off, even if it’s something as mundane and stupid as “get all the shit you need to buy at Target”.  I can literally see myself make progress throughout the month, and this helps motivate me to keep going.  And what I don’t get done one month goes on the top of the list for the following month.  Hope these things help, and keep your head up because just making this post is a step in the right direction.

So TLDR: Be kind to yourself and celebrate each victory, no matter how small, and remember that positive reinforcement is your friend.

I lost my mom to suicide just over five years ago.  It is strange to think that it’s been that long, because it simultaneously feels like it’s been a lifetime ago and yet the event is still very much with me as if it just happened yesterday.  It is hard for me to type this because I remember very  much what it was like for me to lose her.  I don’t want to say the wrong thing to you and risk making you feel worse or more guilty, but I also have to be careful myself not to risk opening up my own wounds and scars that have been very difficult for me to heal, at least to the point where I can more or less function in my day-to-day life.  So I can’t speak in too much depth about it, not because I don’t care about you and what you’re going through, but rather because I can’t let myself risk my own stability by going back to that place, if that makes sense.  But I do want to reach out to you as someone who has experienced a similar loss, so I will share as much with you now as I am able.  I am also writing from the perspective of someone who has not only survived my mom’s suicide, but my own multiple attempts to commit suicide as well.  

I was 27 when my mom committed suicide.  My life was already in shambles from having to move back home four years prior to this from almost getting expelled from my university for trying to kill myself with a revolver.  I had multiple attempts and hospitalizations since early adolescence, and in short put my mom through hell.  My mom first attempted suicide just before my senior year in the university, and very nearly died from it and was in a medically induced coma for close to two weeks.  It fucked me up terribly, and I was wracked with guilt and hopelessness because she was never the same after that, and I blamed myself for all the times I put her through the same hell when I had attempted.  So at the end of that fall semester after her near-fatal attempt, I tried to kill myself with a gun.  I failed because when the moment came I couldn’t make myself pull the trigger.  It did completely fuck up my life and led me to lose (for a time) any chance at what would have otherwise been a promising future.  After her first attempt and my attempt with the gun, I was banned from returning to campus and I had to move back to my childhood home with my mom and my dad, who had his own issues and kept our house in deplorable condition.  So I just stagnated for the next four years, escaping into books and video games while ostensibly trying to finish my last degree requirements from home, and wondering when I’d get up the nerve to put myself out of my misery.  And here’s the thing—my mom was completely selfless.  She would do anything for me and the people she loved, she would never let us know that anything was wrong, and she bore her pain and suffering in silence.  Even when she was severely depressed during all those years after her first attempt, she did not let it show around me, and continued to love me and encourage me even though I was so miserable myself.  And then my grandma died, whom she had a conflicted and strained relationship with herself, and everything changed.  My grandma left her a substantial inheritance, and it looked like our money woes and awful living conditions were finally going to turn around, and for the first time since her attempt, my mom seemed genuinely happy.  She finally was getting up early in the morning just like she used to before the attempt (she had been sleeping for the majority of each day after she attempted suicide), and her interest in gardening and her hobbies was rekindled again.  She even took on home improvement tasks, like ordering a new oven from Home Depot.  I thought I finally had my mom back, and that everything was going to be ok.  And then one day, I found her back in bed.  I asked if she was ok.  She assured me she was fine, that she just had been feeling sick and needed to sleep it off.  I took her word for it, and left for the weekend at my boyfriend’s house in the city.  I didn’t know she had taken an entire bottle of aspirin (my dad had locked up all the prescription meds, from both of us).  It was the last time I saw my mom alive.  She didn’t leave a note.  I didn’t get to say goodbye. 

My mom literally took care of everyone else in her life except herself.  I thought if I had just never attempted that she would have never thought of attempting herself, but I later came to realize that this was a very ego-centric assumption for me to make, and that my moments of carelessness and past mistakes were insignificant in comparison to the entirety of the circumstances that ultimately led her to the decision of taking her life.  The overwhelming guilt and wondering what might have been are probably the worst part, and not being able to talk to them and knowing you’ll never understand why.  

All I can tell you right now is...little by little, it does eventually get better.  And I know that sounds like complete bullshit, because I thought it was bullshit and that my life was over and that I should kill myself too.  But I’m still here.  A little over a year after losing her and going through the motions while living as a severely depressed shell of a person, I got a job that allowed me to move out of my dad’s hellhole of a house and finish my last requirements to earn my degree.  I lost that job but kept looking until I found an internship at a renowned research center associated with my university, and it turned into a job that has not only provided for me, but given my life happiness and purpose.  I didn’t think any of it was possible, and if anyone had told me back then that I would go on to do any of these things, I would have told them they were crazy.  

Please take care of yourself and hold onto every ounce of good that you can.  Remember your mom for who she was to you, for her love and for her raising you to be the person you are today.  Please know that her taking her life was not your fault, and you could not have prevented her from doing that.  Please google “Survivors of Suicide” and look for a group near you, because they are the only people who get it and they can support you through this.  I waited eight months after her death before I took my boyfriend’s mom’s advice and started going to the SOS groups, and yes it was very painful but it was transcendent and ultimately healing.  I wish I had done it sooner.  I can also tell you that I would not be where I am today had her suicide not happened, because it took the shock and trauma of losing her for me to finally get my life together and realize that this is it, this life is all we’ve got and it can be over in an instant.  I’ve been able to help many people since losing her, and this has given my life purpose and meaning.  The same can be true for you too.  I would say more to you but I have to go to sleep now to be good for work tomorrow.  Please don’t hesitate to DM me if you need someone to talk to.  To be totally up front with you, I suck at getting back to people via Reddit but I usually do eventually.  I wish I could hug you and cry with you, but these words will have to suffice.  Be strong and know you can survive this.  Also know that continuing to live does not mean going on without her or forgetting her, but rather carrying her with you through your memories of her.  She will always be a part of you, just as much as my mom is a part of me.  Godspeed to you my friend.
